fact_text: Non-EEA nationals coming to work in Ireland for more than 90 days must have a contract of employment and must apply for the relevant work permission from the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration, DETE, or DFA before arriving. EU/EEA nationals (including Spanish nationals) are explicitly excluded from this requirement and do not need a work permit or employment permit to work in Ireland.
entity_title: Work Permission Requirement for Non-EEA Workers (EU/EEA Exemption)
evidence_quote: Before coming to work in Ireland for more than 90 days, you must have a contract of employment and you must apply for the relevant work permission to the Department of Justice to Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration, the Department of Enterprise, Trade and Employment (DETE) or the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA).

fact_text: The IRP (Irish Residence Permit) registration process managed by Immigration Service Delivery (ISD) applies only to nationals from countries outside the EU, UK, or Switzerland who come to Ireland to work, study, live, or join family for more than 90 days. Spanish nationals as EU citizens are not required to register with ISD under this scheme.
entity_title: ISD Immigration Registration — Scope (Non-EU Nationals Only)
evidence_quote: If you are from a country outside the European Union, UK or Switzerland, and come to Ireland to work, study, live or join family for more than 90 days, you must register with Immigration Service Delivery.

fact_text: Once a non-EEA national successfully registers their immigration permission, they receive an Irish Residence Permit (IRP) card by post. This card is the legal proof that the person is entitled to be in the State. For Spanish and other EU nationals, this card is not issued as they are not required to register.
entity_title: Irish Residence Permit (IRP) Card — Proof of Legal Stay
evidence_quote: When you have successfully registered you will receive an Irish Residence Permit card by post and that is your proof that you are legally in the State.

fact_text: Once ISD grants a permission to stay in Ireland (for non-EEA nationals who need it), the person must register that permission with Irish immigration authorities within 90 days. If an appointment cannot be secured within this period, the permission will not be cancelled while waiting.
entity_title: ISD Registration Deadline — 90 Days After Permission Granted
evidence_quote: Once Immigration Service Delivery (ISD) grants you a permission to stay in Ireland you must register it with the Irish immigration authorities within 90 days. If you cannot get an appointment within this period don't worry – we will not cancel your permission or expect you to leave the country while you are waiting to register.

fact_text: A Personal Public Service (PPS) number is a unique reference number that enables individuals to access social welfare benefits, public services and information in Ireland. It is always 7 numbers followed by either one or two letters and is sometimes referred to as a PPSN.
entity_title: PPS Number — Definition and Format
evidence_quote: Your Personal Public Service (PPS) number is a unique reference number that helps you access social welfare benefits, public services and information in Ireland. A PPS number is always 7 numbers followed by either one or 2 letters. It is sometimes called a PPSN.

fact_text: A PPS number is mandatory when starting work in Ireland — it is needed to register with the Revenue Commissioners. Employers should not ask for a PPS number during recruitment; it is only required when the person actually takes up employment.
entity_title: PPS Number Required When Starting Work
evidence_quote: For example, if you are starting work, you need a PPS number to register with the Revenue Commissioners. However, when you are looking for work, employers should not ask for your PPS number when recruiting. An employer should only ask for your PPS number when you are actually taking up employment with the company.

fact_text: A PPS number is required across a wide range of Irish public services and Revenue schemes including all social welfare services, the Free Travel Pass, registering for school or college, public health services (including the medical card and Drugs Payment Scheme), child immunisation, Revenue schemes such as mortgage interest relief, housing grants, driver theory testing and driving licences.
entity_title: PPS Number — Mandatory Use Cases
evidence_quote: You need your PPS number for: All social welfare services / The Free Travel Pass / Registering for a course in a school or college / Public health services, including the medical card and the Drugs Payment Scheme / Child immunisation / Schemes run by the Revenue Commissioners, such as mortgage interest relief / Housing grants / Driver theory testing and driving licences

fact_text: EU citizens (other than Irish and UK citizens) applying for a PPS number must present their current passport or national identity card as proof of identity. A Spanish national can therefore use their Spanish national identity card (DNI) or passport. A proof of address document not older than 3 months is also required.
entity_title: PPS Number Application — Identity Documents for EU Citizens
evidence_quote: EU citizens (other than Irish and UK): Your current passport or national identity card

fact_text: When applying for a PPS number, an applicant must provide proof of address using a document that shows both name and address and is not older than 3 months. Acceptable documents include: a household utility bill, an official letter or document, a bank statement, or a property lease or tenancy agreement. Third-party confirmation (e.g., from a hotel, hostel, school principal, or accommodation owner) is also accepted.
entity_title: PPS Number Application — Proof of Address Requirements
evidence_quote: You must show proof of your address using any of the following documents (the document must show your name and address and not be older than 3 months): A household utility bill / An official letter or document / A bank statement / Property lease or tenancy agreement / Official confirmation of address by a third party, such as a hotel or hostel administrator or manager, a school principal or administrator, or accommodation or property owner

fact_text: Applicants with a MyGovID account can apply for a PPS number online through MyWelfare. An in-person appointment is still required to complete the verification process. Applications can be made for both an adult and a child in the same application.
entity_title: PPS Number Application — Online via MyGovID
evidence_quote: If you have a MyGovID account, you can apply online for a PPS number on MyWelfare for: An adult / A child / If you are applying for a PPS number for you and your child, you can apply for both at the same time in the same application. You and your child must attend an in-person appointment to complete your application

fact_text: An employer must have the employee's PPS number in order to make PRSI contributions on their behalf. This is a legal requirement; without it, the employer cannot correctly process Pay Related Social Insurance (PRSI) deductions and remittances to Revenue.
entity_title: Employer Needs PPS Number to Make PRSI Contributions
evidence_quote: Your employer needs your Personal Public Service (PPS) number to make PRSI contributions for you.

fact_text: Any person who becomes self-employed in Ireland must register with Revenue as a self-employed person using the Revenue Online Service (ROS). A PPS number is a prerequisite for Revenue registration, and the Tax Reference Number (TRN) after registration is the same as the PPSN.
entity_title: Self-Employment — Mandatory Revenue Registration
evidence_quote: To legally become a sole trader, you must register as self-employed with Revenue. Once you have registered, you pay income tax as a self-employed person, rather than through the PAYE system (which is used for employees). You must have a Personal Public Service (PPS) number to register with Revenue. After you register, your Tax Reference Number (TRN) will be the same as your PPSN.

fact_text: If a person registered for self-assessment since 2015, they are required to file and pay online via ROS (Revenue Online Service). Revenue will not process a paper application (TR1 form) if the applicant is eligible to register online.
entity_title: Revenue Online Service (ROS) — Mandatory Filing for Self-Employed Since 2015
evidence_quote: It is important to note that Revenue will not process a paper application if you are eligible to register online. If you have registered for self-assessment since 2015, you are required to file and pay online.

fact_text: If a self-employed sole trader chooses to trade under a business name (rather than their own name), they must register that business name with the Companies Registration Office (CRO) within one month of adopting the name. The fee is €40 for paper registration (form RBN1) or €20 for online registration via CORE.
entity_title: Business Name Registration — CRO Deadline (1 Month)
evidence_quote: If you want to use a business name, you must register the name with the Companies Registration Office (CRO) within one month of adopting the business name. There is a €40 fee to register a business name using the paper form. There is a €20 fee to register your business name electronically

fact_text: Self-employed persons must keep accounts recording all purchases and sales of goods and services, and all amounts received and paid out. Supporting records must also be kept (e.g., invoices, bank statements, receipts). These records must be retained in case of a Revenue audit.
entity_title: Self-Employment — Mandatory Accounts and Record-Keeping
evidence_quote: You must keep accounts to record: All purchases and sales of goods and services / All amounts received and all amounts paid out / You must also keep supporting records, such as invoices, bank and building society statements, and receipts.

fact_text: Self-employed persons must pay Preliminary Tax (an estimate of the current year's tax liability) on or before 31 October each year. On the same date, they must also file the annual tax return for the previous year and pay any balance of tax due for that year. ROS online filers have a slightly later deadline (18 November 2026).
entity_title: Self-Assessment — Preliminary Tax Deadline 31 October
evidence_quote: You pay Preliminary Tax (an estimate of tax due for your current trading year) on or before 31 October each year and make a tax return for the previous year not later than 31 October. If you pay and file your tax return online using the Revenue Online Service (ROS), the deadline is usually slightly later. In 2026, the extended deadline is 18 November.

fact_text: Self-employed persons must file an income tax return using Form 11 each year, either online via ROS or on paper. Paper filers who submit before 31 August can have Revenue complete the self-assessment section; online filers can accept ROS's calculation or input their own.
entity_title: Self-Assessment — Form 11 Tax Return
evidence_quote: You (or an agent) must make your income tax return and self-assess your tax liability for the previous year. You can: File your Form 11 using the Revenue Online Service (ROS). Certain people must e-file using ROS. / Fill out a paper Form 11 (pdf) and send to Revenue

fact_text: Self-employed traders can claim an Earned Income Tax Credit of up to €2,000 (or 20% of qualifying earned income, whichever is lower). If the person also qualifies for the PAYE Employee Tax Credit, the combined value of both credits cannot exceed €2,000.
entity_title: Self-Employed — Earned Income Tax Credit (2025 onwards)
evidence_quote: In 2025, self-employed traders can claim the lower of either: An Earned Income Tax Credit of €2,000 / A tax credit worth 20% of your qualifying earned income / However, if you also qualify for the PAYE tax credit (for example, if you are an employee of another company, as well as working for yourself), the combined value of these 2 tax credits cannot be more than €2,000.

fact_text: Irish income tax is charged at two rates: 20% (standard rate) up to the standard rate cut-off point of €44,000 for a single person (2025 and 2026), and 40% (higher rate) on income above that point.
entity_title: Income Tax Rates and Standard Rate Cut-Off Points (2025/2026)
evidence_quote: The first part of your income, up to a certain amount, is taxed at 20%. This is known as the standard rate of tax and the amount that it applies to is known as the standard rate tax band. The rest of your income is taxed at the higher rate of tax, 40%. Single person: €44,000 [for 2026 and 2025]

fact_text: Self-employed persons in Ireland pay Class S PRSI contributions directly to the Revenue Commissioners, who then pay the money into the Social Insurance Fund. Revenue sends a record of contributions to the Department of Social Protection.
entity_title: PRSI Class S — Self-Employed Persons
evidence_quote: If you are self-employed, you pay Class S social insurance contributions directly to the Revenue Commissioners. The Revenue Commissioners then pay the money into the Social Insurance Fund. Revenue send a record of the contributions you have paid to the Department of Social Protection.

fact_text: Payment of social insurance (PRSI) is compulsory in Ireland for most employers and employees over 16 years of age. Employment that is liable for social insurance contributions is called insurable employment. The class and rate of PRSI paid depends on the nature of the work and level of earnings.
entity_title: PRSI — Compulsory for Most Employers and Employees
evidence_quote: Most employers and employees (over 16 years of age) pay social insurance (PRSI) contributions into the national Social Insurance Fund. In general, the payment of social insurance is compulsory.

fact_text: From 1 October 2025, unearned income from rents, investments, dividends, and interest on deposits and savings is liable to PRSI at 4.2%. Anyone with unearned income over €5,000 is a chargeable person liable to pay this PRSI charge under Revenue's self-assessment system. People aged under 16 or over 70 are exempt.
entity_title: PRSI on Unearned Income — Rate from October 2025
evidence_quote: From 1 October 2025, unearned income from rents, investments, dividends and interest on deposits and savings is liable to PRSI is at 4.2%. anyone with unearned income of over €5,000 is considered to be a 'chargeable person' and is liable to pay the PRSI at 4.1% on all their unearned income. From 1 October 2025, PRSI increases to 4.2% on all their unearned income.

fact_text: On 1 October 2026, all PRSI contribution rates will increase by 0.15%. This applies across all PRSI classes and is relevant for payroll and self-employed tax planning.
entity_title: PRSI Rate Increase — 1 October 2026
evidence_quote: PRSI rate increase: On 1 October 2026, all PRSI contribution rates will increase by 0.15%.

fact_text: Self-employed persons pay income tax, PRSI, and Universal Social Charge (USC) together under the self-assessment system. Preliminary tax payments made on or before 31 October each year include all three charges. Interest is charged on any late payments.
entity_title: Self-Employed PRSI Paid with Preliminary Tax via Self-Assessment
evidence_quote: When you are registered with Revenue as a self-employed person, you pay income tax, PRSI and the Universal Social Charge under the self-assessment system. This means you pay preliminary tax (an estimate of your income tax, PRSI and Universal Social Charge due for the current year) on or before 31 October each year. You will be charged interest for any late payments.

fact_text: If a Spanish employer sends an employee to work in Ireland for a short assignment, the worker may continue paying social insurance in Spain under EU Regulations for up to 24 months. To benefit from this, an A1 Certificate (formerly E101 Form) must be obtained from the sending country and applied for at least 4 weeks before work begins in Ireland.
entity_title: A1 Certificate Required for Posted Workers (Spain to Ireland)
evidence_quote: If you are employed in Ireland and your employer sends you to work temporarily in another EU state, you will continue to pay PRSI under the Irish system for 24 months. you need an A1 Certificate (formerly E101 Form) to show where you will pay your social insurance. Your employer (or you, if you are self-employed) should apply for an A1 Certificate at least 4 weeks before you start work in another EU country.

fact_text: The Universal Social Charge (USC) applies to all persons whose gross income exceeds €13,000 per year. Once income crosses this threshold, USC is charged on the full income (not just the excess). Social welfare payments and similar payments are exempt.
entity_title: Universal Social Charge (USC) — Income Threshold
evidence_quote: You pay the USC if your gross income is more than €13,000 per year. Once your income is over this limit, you pay the relevant rate of USC on all of your income. If your total income is €13,000 or less per year, you do not pay any USC. If it is more than €13,000 per year, you pay USC on your full income.

fact_text: Self-employed persons pay an extra USC surcharge of 3% on any self-employed income exceeding €100,000 per year, meaning they pay a total of 11% USC on income over €100,000. PAYE employees do not face this surcharge.
entity_title: USC Surcharge for Self-Employed Income Over €100,000
evidence_quote: An extra charge of 3% applies to any self-employed income over €100,000. This means that self-employed people pay a total of 11% USC on any income over €100,000.

fact_text: For self-employed persons, USC is paid as part of the preliminary tax payment due on or before 31 October each year. USC is not reduced by most tax reliefs, meaning it applies to a broader income base than income tax.
entity_title: USC Paid Together with Preliminary Tax (Self-Employed)
evidence_quote: USC: You must pay the Universal Social Charge (USC) if your gross income is over €13,000 in a year. You pay your USC with your preliminary tax payment.

fact_text: Self-employed persons must register for VAT if their annual turnover is, or is likely to be, above the VAT registration threshold. The threshold differs depending on whether the business supplies services or goods and how they are supplied.
entity_title: VAT Registration — Threshold for Self-Employed
evidence_quote: You must register for Value Added Tax (VAT) if your annual turnover is more than, or is likely to be more than, a certain amount. The VAT registration threshold depends on whether you are supplying services or goods and how they are supplied.

fact_text: To be entitled to public health services in Ireland, a person must be ordinarily resident — meaning they have been living in Ireland for at least one year, or intend to live there for at least one year. The HSE may request proof including utility bills, bank statements, rental agreements, or official government documents not older than 12 months.
entity_title: Ordinary Residence — Required for HSE Public Health Services
evidence_quote: You are ordinarily resident if you have been living in Ireland for at least a year or you intend to live here for at least one year. To check that you are ordinarily resident the HSE may ask for: Proof of property purchase or rental / A letter or statement from a financial institution / A current utility bill / A current car or home insurance policy in your name / An official document from a government department The above documents must be dated within the last 12 months.

fact_text: There are two categories of eligibility for ordinarily resident persons in Ireland: Category 1 (full eligibility) for medical card holders and Category 2 (limited eligibility) for those without a medical card. Medical card holders are entitled to free GP services, prescribed drugs, public hospital services, dental/optical/aural services, maternity and infant care, and community care services.
entity_title: Two Tiers of HSE Health Eligibility — Medical Card vs Non-Medical Card
evidence_quote: There are 2 types of eligibility for people who are ordinarily resident in Ireland: Full eligibility for medical card holders / Limited eligibility for people who don't have a medical card / If you have a medical card, you are entitled to free: GP services / Prescribed drugs and medicines, subject to a charge for each item prescribed / Public hospital services / Specific dental, optical and aural services / Maternity and infant care services / Community care and personal social services

fact_text: A Spanish national who is a posted worker (employed in Spain but working temporarily in Ireland) may obtain a medical card in Ireland by providing an E106 (or equivalent S form) from their country confirming participation in the Spanish health insurance scheme. Dependants may also qualify under this pathway.
entity_title: EU Posted Worker Medical Card — E106/S Form Pathway
evidence_quote: If you are a posted worker, working in Ireland, you can get a medical card if you provide an E106 form from your country. Your dependants may also qualify for the medical card if they are not working in Ireland. You will get an S form in your country to confirm that you are part of a health insurance scheme in another EU/EEA country or Switzerland. If your country confirms that you are entitled to healthcare in Ireland, you do not need to complete a financial assessment for a medical card form.

fact_text: An EU/EEA citizen ordinarily resident in Ireland may qualify for a medical card under EU rules if they are receiving a social security pension from another EU/EEA country or Switzerland, or if they are working and paying social insurance in one of those countries, provided they are not also receiving a contributory Irish social welfare payment or liable to PRSI in Ireland.
entity_title: EU Citizen Medical Card — EU Social Security Pension or Payroll Basis
evidence_quote: You may qualify for a medical card under EU rules if you are ordinarily resident in Ireland and you are getting a social security pension from another EU/EEA country or Switzerland, or if you are working and paying social insurance in one of these countries. You must not be in receipt of a contributory Irish social welfare payment or be working in Ireland and be liable to pay PRSI. If you are working in Ireland, you may qualify for a means tested medical card.
